abstract: Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) produced and released by infected macrophages carry both host proteins and bacterial antigens, but whether these components face outward, are enclosed within vesicles, or are associated with co-isolated material remains unclear, limiting our understanding of their accessibility to recipient cells. We combined proteinase K shaving with quantitative proteomics to characterize the protease-accessible proteome of sEVs released by Salmonella-infected RAW264.7 macrophages. Host and bacterial proteins exhibited distinct responses to proteolysis. Of 1,368 proteins quantified, 246 were significantly decreased following digestion and a further 93 became undetectable. Among the depleted proteins, 26 carried independent topological evidence of surface exposure, spanning tetraspanins, integrins, MHC class I molecules, GPI-anchored proteins and membrane receptors, and the depleted fraction also included the immune mediators TNF-, CSF2RA, CD40 and MIF. Most detected Salmonella proteins resisted proteolysis and seven were significantly increased. Peptide-level analysis localized TNF- depletion to its extracellular domain, which fell by more than 3 log? relative to a cytoplasmic peptide measured in the same injection. Preservation of luminal sEV markers and two normalization-independent measures indicated that vesicle integrity was maintained. Despite removal of this protease-accessible fraction, vesicle bioactivity was not diminished: proteinase K-treated vesicles induced stronger Il6 expression and NF-{kappa}B/AP-1 signaling than untreated vesicles, with both responses sensitive to TNF- blockade and polymyxin B. Our findings together suggest that the protease-accessible protein fraction influences the immunostimulatory activity of infection-derived sEV preparations, with removal of the externally available coat of EVs being associated with enhanced inflammatory signaling.
